source.title_on_document: Designing cognitive friction with concept suppression in large language models

supplement.where: The implementation and behavioral-validation appendix is included at PDF p. 37 (printed p. 36), Sections 8.1-8.2.4. Table 5 (repair-training hyperparameters) is on PDF p. 24 (printed p. 23); Tables 6-9 (behavioral-validation excerpts) are on PDF pp. 24-25 (printed pp. 23-24). A separate pipeline reproducibility package is linked at https://github.com/martindisley/utr-concept-suppression-method in PDF p. 14 (printed p. 13), Section 4.1.5 and footnote 4; the repository was not independently inspected.
supplement.holds: The included appendix describes matched behavioral checks of the baseline model and Unlearning to Rest; the associated tables report repair-training hyperparameters and representative model-output excerpts. The separately linked reproducibility package is described as containing full pipeline code, final configuration, concept definition, and an example data schema. No participant-level outcome dataset is identified.

paper_design_summary: Design students and academics (N = 37 analyzed) each spent 15 minutes developing 'proto-concepts' for radically new chairs, written as image-generation prompts, under three within-subject conditions: unaided, with an unmodified Llama 3.2 3B chatbot, and with 'Unlearning to Rest', a Llama 3.2 3B model with the concept 'chair' suppressed. Condition order was randomized by a Latin square. The quantitative outcomes are self-reported NASA-TLX-like workload items and a single perceived-ownership item; the authors state they do not report any empirical analysis of the concept prompts or images.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of three conditions (unaided, Llama3.2:3b, Unlearning to Rest), each completed by every participant
assignment.quote: In order to counterbalance learning effects, participants were assigned these sessions in a random order by the web application, based on a Latin square of conditions and the expected number of participants.

arms.name: Unaided
arms.description: Working alone; chat panel replaced by an open text field for drafting ideas

arms.name: Llama3.2:3b
arms.description: Unmodified Llama 3.2 3B chat model, hosted locally via Ollama

arms.name: Unlearning to Rest
arms.description: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct with weight-level suppression of the concept 'chair' (saliency pruning, vocabulary pruning, repair finetuning)

participants.exclusions: 47 recruited; 38 completed every part, with drop-off attributed to first-cohort students disengaging midway. User 44 from the second cohort was additionally excluded for activity indicating potential misunderstanding or response bias, yielding 37 analyzed. Section 5.2 prints first-cohort N = 31 to N = 26 and second-cohort N = 11; Section 6.2 describes the transcript subset as 11 of the final 37. The paper does not fully reconcile this cohort flow, and the second-cohort count does not establish how many were recruited. The number randomized is not stated.
participants.who: Design students and academics: first cohort, undergraduates in the Diploma in Creative Computing at the Creative Computing Institute, University of the Arts London (in-person classroom workshop); second cohort, postgraduates (MA Interior Design, MA and PhD Design Informatics) at the University of Edinburgh (one-on-one video sessions with think-aloud)
participants.quote: Of the 47 participants that were recruited, only 38 of them completed every part of the study. [...] This yielded a final sample of 37 participants.

ai_tool.name_model: Llama 3.2 3B (meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) unmodified, and 'Unlearning to Rest', the same model with the concept 'chair' suppressed; served through Ollama
ai_tool.how_used: Participants chatted with the model as a conversational ideation partner and could take whole concepts or elements of the conversation; concepts were saved as text-to-image prompts, and images were shown only after the round.

task.description: Develop a series of 'proto-concepts' for the design of radically new chairs, formatted as prompts for an image generator

outcomes.name: Mental Demand (NASA-TLX-like item, 21-point scale)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Self-reported workload after each session; analyzed by repeated-measures ANOVA and BH-corrected paired t-tests. Not scored on the output.

contrasts.reported: Llama3.2:3b 7.24 (3.90) vs Unlearning To Rest 10.19 (4.45) vs Unaided 11.49 (3.80), N = 37; omnibus F = 12.62, df 2, 72, p < .001, partial eta squared = 0.254; Llama3.2:3b < Unlearning To Rest: t = -3.29, pFDR = 0.0050, g = -0.697
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 20 (printed p. 19), Tables 1-3; PDF p. 23 (printed p. 22), Section 6.1

eligibility.reason: Within-subject design with randomized Latin-square condition order meets criterion 1 (PDF p. 17, printed p. 16, Section 5.3). Only 37 people were analyzed (47 recruited, 38 completed, one further participant excluded; PDF p. 16, printed p. 15, Section 5.2), below 50; the three conditions used the same participants. No creativity or diversity outcome is scored on their outputs: quantitative outcomes are self-reported workload and ownership (PDF p. 18, printed p. 17, Section 5.4). The authors explicitly report no empirical analysis of activity outputs (PDF p. 28, printed p. 27, Section 6.4) and state that fixation, novelty, and diversity were not operationalized (PDF p. 35, printed p. 34, Section 7.8). List in the screening report as a small randomized experiment with self-report outcomes; no eligible context class applies.

one_line_finding: With 37 participants, the concept-suppressed model raised self-reported mental demand (10.19 vs 7.24), effort (10.76 vs 7.65), and ownership (9.16 vs 6.38) relative to unmodified Llama 3.2 3B, with no output creativity scored (PDF p. 20, printed p. 19, Tables 1-3; PDF p. 23, printed p. 22, Section 6.1; PDF p. 28, printed p. 27, Section 6.4).
